Anisogrid composite lattice structures consist of geodesic unidirectional composite ribs made by automated wet filament winding.
Developed about 25 years ago for spacecraft applications, Anisogrid structures are now in serial production at the Russian Central Research Institute for Special Machinery.
Traditional carbon-epoxy rib-stringer stiffened airframes typically achieve only 10-20% weight reduction compared to aluminum, with significant cost increases.
The skin in Anisogrid structures is minimized or sometimes omitted because it contributes more to mass than to strength or stiffness.
Optimal cylindrical Anisogrid design depends on six variables: shell thickness, rib angle, rib widths, and rib spacings.
Three design methods are used: geometric programming, safety factor minimization, and numerical optimization.
Finite element analysis with discrete beam-type models is employed for structural analysis including global and local buckling.
Manufacturing steps include forming a silicon rubber coating with grooves, wet winding composite fibers, curing, machining, and removing mandrel and coating.
A Proton-M rocket lattice adapter weighs 50 kg total, with 28 kg being the lattice structure, and can withstand 2 MN axial compressive force.
Anisogrid lattice interstages on Proton-M have achieved about 30% weight reduction compared to aluminum rib-stringer prototypes.
Composite stringers have a g-coefficient of about 0.36 relative to aluminum, while composite skins have g-coefficients of 0.63 to 0.78, indicating skins are less weight efficient.
The allowable tensile strain for unidirectional carbon-epoxy composites is about 1.5%, while allowable compressive strain is about 0.4%.
The integral nature of Anisogrid structures reduces assembly operations and costs compared to traditional composite prepreg lay-ups.
Carbon fiber composite materials cost approximately 12 times more per unit mass than aluminum alloys in wet manufacturing processes.
The Anisogrid concept combines the geodesic structural approach with modern unidirectional composite technology for improved weight and cost efficiency.
Lattice composite fuselage sections can be about 60% lighter than aluminum prototypes.
Flat lattice structures can be used as fuselage rings, wing ribs, stabilizer spars, and cabin floor beams with much higher weight efficiency than aluminum.
The Proton-M rocket has successfully launched eight times with Anisogrid lattice adapters, including a record 5575 kg geosynchronous satellite payload.
The skin in Anisogrid structures mainly serves sealing and safety factor increase, often made from carbon or glass-epoxy fabric composites.
The manufacturing process developed allows for continuous winding without fiber distortion or buildup at nodes, enhancing damage tolerance.
